summary:
Surface Explorer is a web app that helps people use satellite radar to investigate where floodwater may have spread. For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we built interactive maps of Habiganj, Bangladesh, and Chókwè, Mozambique, using observations from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission. Users move a slider to compare radar images of the same area on different dates. In Habiganj, they can also compare areas marked as “possible water” with Landsat imagery and Copernicus flood maps to see where the evidence agrees and where uncertainty remains.

Visual stories and four interactive games help users understand how natural hazards develop before they explore real events on the map. Our goal is to help students and first-time users read satellite imagery, compare evidence, and explain what the data can tell them about a flood.
details:
What is Surface Explorer?

Surface Explorer is a web application that lets people use satellite imagery to investigate how the Earth’s surface changes after a natural disaster. We designed it for people who have never worked with satellite data. Users select an event on an interactive globe, open the affected area on a map, and compare images captured on different dates. In Habiganj, Bangladesh, for example, they can investigate a simple question: “Where might floodwater have spread?”

How does it work?

We used radar observations from NISAR, a joint NASA and ISRO mission, to study flooding in Habiganj, Bangladesh, and Chókwè, Mozambique. NISAR sends radar signals toward the ground and measures how much of the signal returns to the satellite. Radar can observe the ground through clouds that would block an ordinary satellite photograph. Calm water often reflects the signal away from the satellite, so it can appear dark in a radar image.

We used Python to align observations from different dates over the same study area and create map layers showing where the radar signal changed. A Before/After slider lets users compare the same location on two dates. Because several factors can cause a radar image to darken, we label areas that may have flooded as “possible water.” In Habiganj, we compared these areas with Landsat imagery and Copernicus flood maps. Users can see where those sources support the same interpretation and where uncertainty remains. The app shows the observation dates, data sources, and limits of the method.

What makes the project creative?

We combined real satellite observations, six-frame visual stories, and four interactive games in one experience. In the river flood game, users build a levee to protect a village and see how it changes the path of the water. In the ice and rock flood game, they try to stop material moving down a valley. The earthquake game shows how shaking affects buildings, and the wildfire game lets users explore how fire spreads. Each game is labeled as an illustrative simulation. From the story, users can open a real event map and examine what satellites recorded.

What tools did we use, and what impact do we hope to have?

We processed satellite data with Python, built the web interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and used Leaflet and MapLibre for the interactive maps. We considered readability on small screens and used plain language across five languages.

Our goal is to help students and first-time users learn to read satellite maps, compare evidence from several sources, and explain what remains uncertain. By connecting the games to real event maps, Surface Explorer gives users a way to explore how a hazard develops and then investigate what happened in an actual event.
